summary:
Osmolarity counts the particles a solute produces in solution, which is why 150 mM NaCl is 300 mOsm. It returns osmolarity, osmotic pressure and osmotic pressure, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts concentration, osmolality and osmotic pressure, and it handles the dissociation factor that makes salt and sugars behave differently. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: How do I use the Osmolarity / Osmotic Pressure?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: molar concentration of 150 mM, dissociation factor (i) of 2, temperature of 37°C.

Substituting them into the formula gives osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L, osmotic pressure of 773.58 kPa, osmotic pressure of 7.63 atm.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
275 – 295 mOsm/LIsotonicplasma-like; safe for cells
below 275Hypotoniccells swell and can lyse
above 295Hypertoniccells shrink; used for cryopreservation

  • Osmolarity is per litre of solution; osmolality is per kilogram of water. In dilute solutions they are the same; in plasma they differ by about 1%.

  • Osmotic pressure is a colligative property: it depends on particle count, not identity. That is why 150 mM NaCl and 300 mM glucose are both about 300 mOsm.

  • Cell culture media are formulated to 260–320 mOsm/L, and adding a drug stock can push a medium out of range if the stock is concentrated in salt.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Forgetting the dissociation factor for salts.
  • Entering concentration in mmol/L and reading the result as molar.
  • Using 8.314 with pressure in atm.

faq.q: What is the osmolarity of normal saline?
faq.a: 154 mM NaCl × 2 = 308 mOsm/L, close to plasma at about 290.

faq.q: Why is osmolality used in clinical work?
faq.a: Because it is measured per kilogram of water, which does not change with temperature or with the volume the solute displaces.

faq.q: What does the Osmolarity / Osmotic Pressure actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns osmolarity, osmotic pressure and osmotic pressure. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
